sentences.text:
(16-01-2020)
1. Applicant has filed this criminal revision under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure being aggrieved by the judgment dated 01.02.2000 passed by the appellate Court I Additional Sessions Judge, Shahdol in Criminal Appeal No. 124/97 whereby learned appellate Court upheld the conviction and sentence passed by the Court of learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Shahdol by judgment dated 02.08.1997 in Criminal Case No. 832/96 whereby learned trial Court convicted the applicant for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereafter referred to in the order as ''PFA Act'') and sentenced to undergo S.I for 6 months.
and one thousand rupees fine, with default stipulation.

2. The case of the prosecution against the applicant in short is that applicant was having mixed milk in the container and going to sell and distribute mixed milk, food inspector J. P. Verma introduced himself and purchased mixed milk from the applicant, mixed the same with formalin, prepared three samples and after performing all the formalities sent one sample to the public analyst State Food Laboratory and State Food Laboratory found the mixed milk adulterated and not found as per standard laid down under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.
The Food Inspector after being given notice to the applicant submitted a complaint before the Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class.

entities.text: Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
After completion of trial, delivered the judgment on 02.08.1997 found the applicant violated of the provision of Section 7(1)(2)(1)(a)(m) of the PFA Act and convicted the applicant under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the PFA Act and sentenced him to undergo S.I. for 6 months Premlal Yadav vs The State Of M.P. on 16 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/152767904/
1 and one thousand rupees fine, with default stipulation.

entities.text: Premlal Yadav vs The State Of M.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 3. The applicant being aggrieved by that conviction and sentence preferred an appeal which was registered as Criminal Appeal No.124/1997.
Learned appellate Court after hearing both the parties delivered the judgment on 01.02.2000 while dismissing the appeal affirmed the conviction and sentence passed by the trial Court.

Hence, the applicant filed this criminal revision being aggrieved by that conviction and sentence passed by both the Courts below solely on the ground that learned trial Court not appreciated the evidence in proper perspective.
Independent witness Rajendra Prasad not supported the case of prosecution and denied for the purchase of milk by food inspector.
Learned trial Court not appreciated the evidence of this witness properly.
Food Inspector had not complied with the provision of Section 13(2) of the PFA Act.
It is the mandatory provision.

Learned trial Court failed to observe that which specification of the milk was not as per the standard of mixed milk as provided in PFA Rules, 1955 and without considering this fact, learned trial Court as well as appellate Court convicted the applicant.
The judgment of both the Courts below have committed legal and factual error,hence, it has been prayed to allow this petition and acquit the applicant of the said charges.
4. Learned Panel Lawyer for the respondent/State on the other hand submitted that the appellate Court affirmed the conviction and sentence.
It is a concurrent finding.
In revision, the Court should not appreciate the evidence as appreciated in the appellate Court.
There was public analyst report on the record.
Specific notice of 13(2) of the PFA Act had been sent to the applicant on the registered address but applicant had received that notice.
Learned trial Court presumed the service of that notice.
Hence, prayed to dismiss the revision.
5. Having heard both the counsel and having perused record of both Courts below.
Perused the statements of witnesses.
Food Inspector J. P. Verma (PW-1) recorded his statement before the Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class.

This witness categorically stated that after preparing one sample sent to the public analyst by registered post along with form no.7.This witness categorically exhibited public analyst report as Ex.P/13.
Perused Ex.P/13

. In the mixed milk, the fat was 2.4%,
solid not fat 4.1% found and starch was absent.
On these specification public analyst found the sample adulterated.

This witness categorically stated that he sent the notice to the applicant by post and Ex.P/15 is the postal receipt.
6.

Witness S. D. Choudhary (PW-3) who is the subordinate staff of Deputy Director Food and Drug Administration, Shahdol clearly stated that the notice along with copy of the public analyst under Section 13(2) of the PFA Act had been sent by the office.
This witness submitted the notice Ex.P/16 and postal receipt Ex.P/17 and categorically stated that notice not received back to the office.
The notice sent to the postal address of the applicant had not been received back, it is presumed that notice had been served on the applicant.
The applicant did not cross-examine this witness on this point meaning thereby, this fact is un-rebutted and can be admitted.

This Court is of the view that learned both Courts below not committed any error in presuming that the report of the public analyst under Section 13(2) of the PFA Act has been served to the applicant.

sentences.text: So far specifications of mixed milk are concerned, standard of mixed milk is provided in PFA Rules, 1955.
According to that, mixed milk should contain not less than 4.5% milk fat and 8.5% milk solid not fat in all over India.
The public analyst report Ex.P/13 showed in sample 2.4% milk fat and found 4.1% milk solid not fat.
No doubt mixed milk was found to be adulterated.
8. The applicant has been convicted and sentenced by trial Court and this conviction and sentence has been affirmed by the appellate Court as per Section 393.
This conviction and sentence attained finality.
In this revision, the Court is having a limited scope of re-appreciation of evidence.
Perused the statement of PW2 who is independent witness.

This witness categorically stated that he don't know the applicant and denied the signatures on Ex.P/5 and P/6 and categorically stated that food inspector neither took the samples nor prepared a panchnama.

After considering the whole statements of this witness, no doubt that this witness neither supported the case of the applicant nor supported the case of the prosecution but so far as food inspector is concerned, there is nothing on record that he is having a motive to implicate the applicant falsely.
In these circumstances, the learned Court not erred in believing the statements of food inspector.

9. Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Kishan Rao vs. Shankargouda, (2018) 8 SCC 165, while reiterating the ambit and scope of re-appreciation of evidence under Section 397 read with 401 of Cr.P.C. when conviction and sentence affirmed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge in appeal,
has held in paras 12 to 14 as hereunder:
12.
This Court has time and again examined the scope of Section 397 /401 Cr.P.C. and the ground for exercising the revisional jurisdiction by the High Court.

In State of Kerala vs. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri , 1999 (2) SCC 452, while considering the scope of the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court this Court has laid down the following:
"5......In its revisional jurisdiction, the High Court can call for and examine the record of any proceedings for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order.

entities.text: State of Kerala vs. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri , 1999 (2) SCC 452
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In other words, the jurisdiction is one of supervisory jurisdiction exercised by the High Court for correcting miscarriage of justice.
But the said revisional power cannot be equated with the power of an appellate court nor can it be treated even as a second appellate jurisdiction.

Ordinarily, therefore, it would not be appropriate for the High Court to reappreciate the evidence and come to its own conclusion on the same when the evidence has already been appreciated by the Magistrate as well as the Sessions Judge in appeal,
unless any glaring feature is brought to the notice of the High Court which would otherwise tantamount to gross miscarriage of justice.

On scrutinizing the impugned judgment of the High Court from the aforesaid standpoint, we have no hesitation to come to the conclusion that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the conviction of the respondent by reappreciating the oral evidence....."

sentences.text: Another judgment which has also been referred to and relied by the High Court is the judgment of this Court in Sanjaysinh Ramrao Chavan vs. Dattatray Gulabrao Phalke and others, 2015 (3) SCC 123.

entities.text: Sanjaysinh Ramrao Chavan vs. Dattatray Gulabrao Phalke and others, 2015 (3) SCC 123
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This Court held that the High Court in exercise of revisional jurisdiction shall not interfere with the order of the Magistrate unless it is perverse or wholly unreasonable or there is non- consideration of any relevant material, the order cannot be set aside merely on the ground that another view is possible.

Following has been laid down in paragraph 14:
"14.....Unless the order passed by the Magistrate is perverse or the view taken by the court is wholly unreasonable or there is non- consideration of any relevant material or there is palpable misreading of records, the Revisional Court is not justified in setting aside the order, merely because another view is possible.
The Revisional Court is not meant to act as an appellate court.
The whole purpose of the revisional jurisdiction is to preserve the power in the court to do justice in accordance with the principles of criminal jurisprudence.
The revisional power of the court under Sections 397 to 401 CrPC is not to be equated with that of an appeal.

Unless the finding of the court, whose decision is sought to be revised, is shown to be perverse or untenable in law or is grossly erroneous or glaringly unreasonable or where the decision is based on no material or where the material facts are wholly ignored or where the judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or capriciously, the courts may not interfere with decision in exercise of their revisional jurisdiction."
14. In the above case also conviction of the accused was recorded, the High Court set aside the order of conviction by substituting its own view.
This Court set aside the High Court's order holding that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in substituting its views and that too without any legal basis.

10. In these circumstances, this Court is of the view that learned trial Court while convicting the applicant for minimum prescribed punishment, this Court is not inclined to interfere in that minimum punishment.
11. Consequently, this revision being devoid of merit is hereby dismissed.
There shall be no order as to costs.

(Vishnu Pratap Singh Chauhan)
